Can six ability scores tell a hero from a villain?¶

Shared code¶

Setup used by every section: the six input columns, the cleaning rules of Section 2, the fixed colours from the brief, and the confusion-matrix / figure helpers. Everything uses random_state=42.

Section 2 · Data Preparation (10 marks)¶

Both files are cleaned with the same fixed rules, in this order:

# Step Applies to
1 Inspect — shape, columns, dtypes, missing counts (T1) train.csv and test.csv
2 Remove duplicates — same name twice → keep first; name in both files → drop from train.csv both
3 Mark missing — 6 scores numeric; blanks and 0 → NaN (0 means unknown) both
4 Remove weak rows — 3 or more of the 6 scores missing → drop both
5 Fill the gaps — training median, inside each task's Pipeline training data only

The cleaning functions are defined once in the Shared code section above, so every task uses exactly the same rules.

G1: heroes outnumber villains roughly 3 : 2 in both files. A model that always says "Hero" would already be right about 61 % of the time on test.csv, which is why accuracy alone is misleading and Macro-F1 is the main metric.

T5: KNN has the best test Macro-F1 (0.526), well ahead of the Decision Tree (0.408) and the Baseline (0.378). The Baseline has the highest accuracy (0.609) only because it calls everyone a hero and finds zero villains, so accuracy would have picked the worst model.

Step 6 · Report¶

G2: the tree predicts "Hero" for almost everyone: it labels 120 of 137 heroes correctly but catches only 6 of 88 villains (82 villains missed), so its villain recall is just 0.068.

G3: KNN is more balanced: it catches 29 of 88 villains (recall 0.330) while still labelling 100 of 137 heroes correctly. It is clearly better than the tree at finding villains, but it still misses two out of three.

G4: the Baseline wins only on accuracy, because always saying "Hero" is right 61 % of the time. On every macro metric KNN is clearly best, while the tree's Macro-Recall (0.472) is even below the Baseline's 0.500.

Comparison basis¶

  1. Winner: highest test Macro-F1. 2. Tie-break: gap < 0.01 → higher Villain recall. 3. Useful? only if test Macro-F1 > Baseline's. 4. Overfitting? Train Macro-F1 − Test Macro-F1 > 0.10.
Macro-F1 gap between the two models: 0.118 -> winner: KNN
  Train Macro-F1 Test Macro-F1 Recall Villain Gain over Baseline Useful? (> Baseline) Train − Test gap Overfits? (gap > 0.10)
Model              
Baseline 0.391 0.378 0.000 0.000 - 0.013 no
Decision Tree 0.563 0.408 0.068 0.030 yes 0.155 yes
KNN 0.739 0.526 0.330 0.148 yes 0.213 yes

Answers¶

Q1 · Which model wins by the rules? KNN (k = 3, uniform weights). Its test Macro-F1 is 0.526, against 0.408 for the Decision Tree. The gap is 0.118, far more than 0.01, so no villain-recall tie-break is needed (KNN would win that too: 0.330 vs 0.068).

Q2 · Did both models beat the Baseline? By how much? Yes, both are above the Baseline's test Macro-F1 of 0.378, so both count as "useful" by the rule. KNN beats it by +0.148; the Decision Tree only by +0.030, which is small. Its accuracy (0.560) is actually lower than the Baseline's 0.609.

Q3 · Which class is harder to predict? Villains. In G2 the tree finds only 6 of 88 villains (recall 0.068, F1 0.108) but 120 of 137 heroes (recall 0.876, F1 0.708). In G3 KNN finds 29 of 88 villains (recall 0.330, F1 0.377) and 100 of 137 heroes (recall 0.730, F1 0.676). Villains are the minority class, and their ability scores overlap heavily with heroes', so both models lean towards predicting "Hero".

Q4 · Does either model overfit? By the rule (Train − Test Macro-F1 > 0.10), both do. The Decision Tree drops from 0.563 on train to 0.408 on test (gap 0.155). KNN drops from 0.739 to 0.526 (gap 0.213); with k = 3 each training character is one of its own three nearest neighbours, so its training score is inflated. The tree's test score is also well below its CV score (0.540), so its chosen splits did not generalise to test.csv.

Step 3 · Build Network A and Network B¶

G12 · Architecture diagrams — Network A and Network B (drawn as a diagram, the only graph not made by code)

Step 4 · Train¶

Same data and same settings for both networks; early stopping watches validation loss and restores the best epoch's weights. Each network is rebuilt from seed 42 right before it trains, so both start from the same random state and the run is repeatable.

Network A: ran 166 epochs, best epoch 151, lowest validation loss 0.6208
Network B: ran 72 epochs, best epoch 57, lowest validation loss 0.6332

T9: the two networks share every setting except the hidden layers. Network A kept improving slowly and reached its lowest validation loss at epoch 151 (stopped at 166); Network B peaked much earlier, at epoch 57 (stopped at 72), and its best validation loss (0.633) is worse than A's (0.621).

G13: both of Network A's curves fall quickly in the first ~20 epochs, then flatten at about 0.62–0.63 and stay close together, with no rising validation curve. That points to a good fit with mild underfitting: the network has learned what little the six scores offer (a model that always predicts the 36 % villain rate scores about 0.65).

G14: Network B's training loss keeps falling after epoch 57 while its validation loss creeps back up slightly, a small sign of overfitting. Early stopping caught it and restored the epoch-57 weights. Both losses still sit as high as Network A's, so the extra layer did not find more signal.

Step 6 · Compare¶

Network A vs Network B: winner = higher test Macro-F1; "the deeper network improved results" only if B is at least 0.01 higher. Overfitting = train − test Macro-F1 > 0.10, or validation loss rising while training loss falls.

Network B − Network A test Macro-F1 = -0.033 -> the deeper network did NOT improve results

T11: KNN ranks first (Macro-F1 0.526), followed by Network A (0.455), Network B (0.421), the Decision Tree (0.408) and the Baseline (0.378). No pair is within 0.01, so the villain-recall tie-break is never needed, and all four real models beat the Baseline, though Network B and the tree only narrowly.

G16: on accuracy the five models sit within 0.06 of each other (0.56–0.62), and the Baseline and both networks are near the top simply by predicting "Hero". Macro-F1 separates them clearly, and KNN is the only model that does noticeably better than guessing at telling villains apart.

Answers¶

Q9 · Did Network B beat Network A by at least 0.01 Macro-F1? No. Network B scored 0.421 against Network A's 0.455 on test.csv, 0.033 lower, so the deeper network did not improve results. The six scores carry little signal about alignment, so extra capacity has nothing more to learn. With 257 weights and only 732 training rows, B instead starts fitting noise sooner: its training loss keeps falling after epoch 57 while validation loss rises, and its best validation loss (0.633) is worse than A's (0.621).

Q10 · Do the loss curves show over- or underfitting? Which epoch was best? Neither network overfits by the Macro-F1 rule (train − test gap 0.040 for A, 0.064 for B). The curves mostly show mild underfitting: training and validation loss flatten together around 0.62–0.63, only a little below the 0.65 a no-information model gets. Network B also shows a small overfitting tail (validation loss creeping up while training loss falls), which early stopping removed. Best epochs: 151 for Network A and 57 for Network B.

Q11 · Did either network beat the Decision Tree and KNN? Both networks beat the Decision Tree (0.408): A by +0.047, B by +0.013. Neither beat KNN (0.526): A is 0.071 behind and B 0.105 behind. The networks also learned from only 80 % of train.csv (732 rows), while the tree and KNN used all 916.

Q12 · Two limitations of this dataset or experiment

  1. The six ability scores are weak, noisy evidence of alignment. Whether a character is a hero or villain comes from story, not power level, and the scores are rough estimates where many unknowns were recorded as 0 (86 train characters were dropped for having 3+ unknown scores). Even the best model finds only a third of villains.
  2. The data is small and imbalanced. There are 916 training and 225 test characters, with only 88 villains in test, so a few changed predictions move recall and Macro-F1 noticeably. The networks are judged on one fixed 80/20 split and one seed, and with no class weights or resampling allowed, every model leans towards the majority "Hero" class.
